verdicts.critic:
Neutrality holds across most of this draft, and the crux is the strongest I have reviewed on this dimension. All nine camps are steelmanned in their own voice, each gets exactly one action, no section carries a house verdict, and the questions concede against themselves symmetrically (the ban question explicitly notes that displacement "is so far a prediction rather than a measured finding" — a real concession by the skeptic side, not balance theatre). Prevalence weights track legislative and literature footprint rather than editorial sympathy, and the basics carry the asymmetry honestly: three hard-outcome rise stats sit beside the Orben null and a PISA item whose own detail names the contradicting HBSC series.

The crux passes cleanly. The lead ("Everyone is reading the same average, and no two camps agree on what it is an average of") is a declarative naming an axis, not a question with an or-fork, and not a verdict. Every camp locates itself in the subtitle: no effect (Weak Evidence), a real cause blurred by crude exposure measures (Great Rewiring), the wrong exposure (Design), the wrong unit because how is teachable (Media Skills), a cause elsewhere (Social Determinants), a widened definition (Prevalence Inflation), concentrated harm (Vulnerable Subgroup), and the two camps for whom effect size is beside the point (Parental Authority, Digital Rights). It is not a binary, and it does not say both sides have a point.

The missing-camp search surfaced no unrepresented camp. WebSearch budget was spent, so I ran the fallback: Wikipedia's landscape article and The Anxious Generation reception section, plus the camps' own umbrella orgs. Candidates it raised — industry self-regulation, the Goldilocks/moderate-use reading, problematic-use clinicians, the play-and-education critics (Peter Gray, Mike Masnick), the moral-panic reading (Taylor Lorenz), the diagnostic-coding critique (Wallace-Wells) — all locate inside an existing position.

What blocks is factual, and it lands asymmetrically on one camp. The Engagement Design Critic's legal footprint is described wrongly in the direction that weakens it. The Ninth Circuit's 12 March 2026 CAADCA ruling was substantially favorable to the state — it vacated the blanket injunction and the age-estimation injunction and revived the default-privacy and geolocation provisions, affirming the injunction only as to several data-use and dark-patterns terms it found vague (EPIC and Courthouse News both report it as a reprieve for the law; Tech Policy Press gives the holding). The draft calls it "largely held unconstitutional" and says the Act "has never taken effect." Worse, the same paragraph's framing — statutes enjoined, settlement carried the agenda — omits that the Ninth Circuit upheld California's SB 976 addictive-feed ban and default-private settings for minors on 9 September 2025, and those provisions remain enforceable. That is the design camp's live statute, and its absence is what makes the "courts kept it out" narrative look true.

Separately, the Meta settlement is reported as "29 states." State attorney general announcements and PBS put it at 47 states and about $17 billion over ten years (DC's AG: up to $17.1 billion); the WSJ and CNN report 48 states and $18 billion. Only one aggregator headline says 29. The figure appears twice, including in the camp's prevalence_basis, so it is load-bearing.

Everything else I could reach checked out verbatim: the Trevor Project's 68/52/40 and 8%-to-20% figures, YMCA's 73% youth services cut, Braghieri/Levy/Makarin's Facebook rollout finding and its social-comparison mechanism, Beyens' 2,155 assessments and 44/46/10 split, Orben and Przybylski's 355,358 adolescents and 0.4%, the AAP Center's "complicated and personal" framing and its co-directors, Toscano's parental-consent-as-anchor quote (IFS, 28 August 2026), the 6 July 2026 Supreme Court denial on the Texas app-store law, and the July 2026 eSafety finding at three months into Australia's ban.

blocking.issue: The Ninth Circuit's March 2026 ruling on California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act is described backwards, in the direction that weakens the Engagement Design Critic camp. The court vacated the injunction against the Act as a whole and against its age-estimation requirement, reviving the provisions requiring highest-privacy-by-default for children and limits on collecting children's geolocation data; it affirmed the injunction only as to several data-use and dark-patterns restrictions it found unconstitutionally vague, and remanded to N.D. Cal. EPIC headlined it as allowing parts of the design code to go into effect and Courthouse News as another reprieve for the law. Calling it 'largely held unconstitutional' and saying the Act 'has never taken effect' misstates a load-bearing fact about one camp's legal standing.
blocking.fix: Replace with what the court did: '…enjoined in 2023 and again in 2025, then partly revived in March 2026, when the Ninth Circuit vacated the blanket injunction and its age-estimation holding, reinstating the default-privacy and geolocation provisions while leaving several data-use and dark-pattern rules enjoined as unconstitutionally vague.' Drop 'it has never taken effect'.
blocking.quote: Engagement Design Critic, detail paragraph 2: “California’s Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, signed in 2022, is the clearest drafted expression of the design-first position, requiring safer default settings and barring manipulative interface patterns aimed at minors without setting an access floor by age at all, though it has never taken effect: enjoined in 2023 and again in 2025, and largely held unconstitutional by the Ninth Circuit in March 2026.”

blocking.issue: The design camp's prevalence_basis rests on a false premise — that courts have kept design statutes from operating and that only a settlement carried the agenda. It omits the design camp's statute that is actually in force: on 9 September 2025 the Ninth Circuit upheld California's Protecting Our Kids from Social Media Addiction Act (SB 976), sustaining both the ban on serving addictive feeds to minors without parental consent (rejecting the argument that the term was vague) and the default-private-account requirement as a content-neutral safety measure; those provisions remain enforceable pending trial (the engagement-metrics/like-count provision was struck). Understating a camp's real-world footprint is a neutrality defect, not just an omission.
blocking.fix: Correct the prevalence_basis to record a design statute in force, e.g. add: 'and California’s SB 976, whose ban on addictive feeds for minors without parental consent and default-private settings the Ninth Circuit upheld in September 2025 and which remains enforceable pending trial.' Then soften 'Where statutes were enjoined, settlement carried the agenda' to 'Settlement carried the agenda further still', so the sentence no longer asserts that the statutory route failed.

State AG announcements of 26 August 2026 (DC, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and others) and PBS put the settlement at 47 states and about $17 billion over ten years, with DC's AG describing up to $17.1 billion; the Wall Street Journal and CNN report 48 states and $18 billion. blocking.fix: Replace '29 states' with the figure the attorneys general themselves announced — '47 states' — in both the detail and the prevalence_basis, and align the amount with the same source ('about $17 billion, payable over ten years'; state announcements put it at up to $17.1 billion). The tech industry appears in this draft only as antagonist or defendant: leaked research, dark patterns, litigating against statutes, opposing the app-store route. verdicts.critic:
Fact-source review of the Basics stats (my slice only; prose claims left to the claim ledger). I verified all 12 sourced stats — headline value, note, detail figures, series values, source label, URL and date — by fetching each cited source directly (WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of my run, so every check ran through WebFetch or curl against primary sources, plus CrossRef/EuropePMC for bibliographic identity). Nothing came back wrong, misattributed, dead, undated or stale. No blocking defects.

What was confirmed, source by source:
1. YRBS girls' persistent sadness — CDC 2023 results page gives 57% (2021) → 53% (2023); the 2011 MMWR surveillance summary (SS-61-4) gives 35.9% female / 21.5% male verbatim; the 2011–2021 Data Summary & Trends Report gives male 29% in 2021. Series and both source links resolve and support their own numbers.
2. Suicide, ages 10–14 — NCHS Data Brief 471 states the rate "tripled from 2007 through 2018" (0.9 → 2.9), 1.3 in 2001, and for 10–24 "increased 62% from 2007 through 2021 (from 6.8 deaths per 100,000 to 11.0)". Exact match, correct brief number and publisher.
3. ED visits for self-harm — Mercado et al., JAMA 2017: girls 10–14 rose ~110 (2009) to 318 (2015) per 100,000, APC 18.8%; males 10–14 44.1 per 100,000 in 2015 with no significant trend (APC 1.0, ns). The "Boys 44" series value and "rates for boys did not rise" both check out.
4. Orben & Przybylski — the accepted manuscript (Oxford ORA copy, located via the Semantic Scholar record for the DOI) states "at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being", and the specification counts 372 (YRBS), 40,966 (MTF), 20,004 selected (MCS) appear verbatim. Bullying, getting into fights and getting enough sleep are all comparison specifications, so the comparison in the note is the paper's own. The subset curves also support the "social media specifically" line (MTF complete SCA median β = -.005 vs social-media-only -.031; MCS -.032 vs -.056).
5. Pew smartphone access — 95% overall, 98% ages 15–17, 90% ages 13–14, fieldwork Sept 18–Oct 10 2024; the 73% decade-earlier baseline is verified in Pew's own April 2015 report ("Some 73% of teens have access to smartphones").
6. Pew "almost constantly" — the Dec 9 2025 report gives 40%, 36% using at least one platform almost constantly, TikTok 21%, YouTube 20%, Instagram 12%, Snapchat 12%; the 46% (2024) is Pew's own published figure for the 2024 report and 24% (2015) is the baseline Pew itself cites.
7. PISA loneliness — Twenge et al. 2021 abstract: "School loneliness increased 2012-2018 in 36 out of 37 countries", nearly twice as many adolescents with elevated loneliness, n = 1,049,784. The counterweight in the detail is also right: Cosma et al., J Adolesc Health 2020, 36 countries, 2002–2018, "do not provide evidence for substantial declines in mental well-being".
8. NSCH anxiety/depression — Lebrun-Harris et al., JAMA Pediatrics 2022: anxiety 7.1% → 9.2% (+29%), depression 3.1% → 4.0% (+27%), NSCH 2016–2020. Exact.
9. Pew teen attitudes — 48% mostly negative for peers (32% in 2022), 11% positive, 41% neither, 14% personally negative, 30% helps / 7% hurts friendships, 45% too much time, 45% hurts sleep, 19% own mental health, 44% of concerned parents. Every number in note, detail and series matches.
10. Sleep — Echevarria et al., Sleep Medicine: X 2023 (2004 Pelotas cohort, n = 1,949 / 1,851): ≥9 h screen time associated with 32.4 fewer minutes of sleep vs <2 h and 60% higher likelihood of poor sleep quality.
11. Cellphone laws — Ballotpedia (fetched via curl; the page renders empty to WebFetch) says verbatim: "As of August 27, 2026, 45 states had enacted laws or policies… 36 states ban or limit cellphones in classrooms", plus five requiring districts to adopt a policy and four encouraging limits. Florida is listed first at May 9, 2023, and Illinois SB 2427 (signed July 28, 2026) does permit high schoolers phones at lunch and between classes.
12. Australia — the AP/PBS piece (Jan 16 2026) reports about 4.7 million accounts "deactivated or restricted", the ten named platforms, A$49.5m fines, "reasonable steps", Dec. 10 2025 start, and the eSafety Commissioner as the regulator that received the platform reports and released the tally, so the source label is fair.

Vintage: the 2013–2023 YRBS Data Summary is still CDC's most recent (no 2025 release listed); Pew's publication list shows no 2026 successor to either teens report used here; Ballotpedia's own as-of date matches the draft's. Durability is sound: the load-bearing items are structural (trend series, mortality, effect size, near-saturated ownership) and the genuinely perishable ones (Australia's rollout, state counts) are each dated in the note and parked at tier 3.

notes: GROUNDING: before judging I read /home/jeff/Documents/Projects/InfinityProject/Ideya/templates/topics/components/_stat_tile.html and _position.html plus static/css/ideya.css to fix the compact/expanded boundary exactly. Stat glance = label + viz/series + note (detail AND source_label sit inside .tmore, behind the expand). Position glance = name + steelman ONLY — .pdesc lives inside .pmore, so `description` is EXPANDED layer, not compact. That is stricter than the brief implied, and I judged positions on their six steelmen alone.

VERDICT: the above-fold compact layer is self-sufficient. A reader who never opens anything leaves with: reported teen distress up sharply since ~2010 across self-report, mortality and hospital measures and concentrated in girls; exposure near-universal and near-continuous; the best-known measured association is tiny (0.4%); and restriction is spreading fast (39 states, Australia’s 4.7M accounts). Question 1’s text and why supply the load-bearing caveat that timing overlap is undisputed while causation is not, and question 5’s why supplies the caveat that policy has outrun evaluation. No above-fold line asserts causation. That is parity.

SELECTION — basics: the 9 tier-1 tiles are the right 9 and the boundary is a genuine drop-off. The three trend stats are not redundant: sadness is self-report survey, suicide rate is death-certificate mortality, ER self-harm is hospital record — three independent measurement families, which is exactly what the measurement-artifact question turns on. The T2/T3 remainder (parent-reported anxiety diagnoses, teens’ own verdict on social media, sleep minutes at 9+ hours) are all genuinely secondary; the sleep tile at T3 is correctly last, being non-US and about screen time generally rather than social media.

SELECTION — questions: 6/7 above fold, and the one demoted (measurement/help-seeking inflation) is the right demotion: it is the only question that does not bear on what to do. Boundary is a real drop-off.

SELECTION — positions: the six above the fold cover causation-yes, causation-weak, mechanism-is-design, parents-decide, harm-is-concentrated, and restriction-harms-the-vulnerable. That spans the debate. Social Determinants Camp (prevalence 40) is the most arguable omission — it is the only camp offering an affirmative rival cause for the post-2010 rise — but positions render by prevalence_weight, so promoting it means raising a prevalence claim (fact-adjacent, outside presentation scope), and it would displace Digital Rights Defender, which is the necessary counterweight to question 6 on age verification. The current six are the right six. Not a defect.

CONSEQUENCE of that omission, worth the human knowing: above the fold, the ONLY carrier of ‘something other than phones could explain the rise’ is one clause in question 1’s why (‘the same decade brought many other candidate causes that correlational data cannot separate out’). It is load-bearing out of proportion to its length. Protect that clause in any later trim — if it goes, five above-fold stats document a rise with no above-fold account of any alternative cause.

LABEL SCOPE — stat 1 is the one real drift. Label reads ‘Persistent sadness or hopelessness · teen girls, CDC survey’ while the note (same compact layer) correctly says ‘US high school girls’. YRBS samples grades 9–12; ‘teen girls’ reads broader. In this topic that matters more than usual, because the two neighboring tiles are explicitly ‘ages 10 to 14’ and question 2 above the fold asks whether harm concentrates by age — a scanner could take 53% as covering 10-to-14s, which the value does not measure. Non-blocking because the note fixes it in the same always-visible layer, but the cheap fix is a label edit to ‘Persistent sadness or hopelessness · US high school girls (CDC survey)’.

LABEL SCOPE — two milder cases, both resolved by their notes, both optional: stat 4 ‘Share of wellbeing differences linked to tech use’ does not say the population is adolescents (note says ‘teenagers’); stat 7 ‘Teens online almost constantly’ does not say US (note says ‘US teens’). Checked all twelve stats; every other label states its denominator and scope correctly, and stat 8’s value/unit (39 · states) correctly excludes the District of Columbia that its note adds.

SOURCE VISIBILITY, a design consequence rather than a draft defect: source_label renders only behind the expand, so a stat’s attribution survives the glance only if the label or note carries it. Eight of nine above-fold tiles do (Orben & Przybylski and PISA in labels, CDC/Pew/Education Week in labels or notes). Stat 3 (ER self-harm) is the exception — neither its label nor its note names JAMA or Mercado, and ‘Published in JAMA in 2017’ sits in the detail. If the human wants consistency, appending ‘(JAMA, 2017)’ to that note would match the rest of the set. No mislead either way.

EXPANDED-LAYER denominator, flagged for whoever owns that layer since it is outside my compact remit: Vulnerable Subgroup Researcher’s description reads ‘Across 2,155 real-time reports from Dutch adolescents, 44% felt no different… 46% felt better and 10% felt worse’. The 2,155 counts assessments; the 44/46/10 are percentages of adolescents, as the detail correctly states. The closing clause ‘a near-zero average built from people it fits badly’ resolves it, so the reader lands right — but ‘44% of them felt no different’ would remove the ambiguity, and the person-versus-moment distinction is the camp’s entire claim.

One steelman leans on an allusion: Weak Evidence Methodologist’s ‘the effect is the size of eating potatoes’. With descriptions behind the expand, that phrase plus ‘it shrinks the harder you look’ is the whole compact statement of the main skeptic camp. It survives because ‘potatoes’ plainly reads as trivial and the 0.4% tile sits above the fold in Basics to anchor it — but it is the one above-fold position line doing work by implication rather than statement.
